title: Electric field strength and field lines; Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium
qualification: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: F08-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; F03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; F08-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; F08-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: F03-1#N.2, F08-1#N.3b, F08-ap1#N.12, F03-1#N.7b, F08-1#N.7b, F08-ap1#N.2, F03-1#N.11, F08-1#N.8, F08-ap1#N.5, F08-ap1#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Excess charge
items.clue: Net surplus that sits entirely on the outer surface of a metal.

items.label: Neutral point
items.clue: Place between two like charges where E = 0, nearer the smaller one.

items.label: Insulator
items.clue: Material where charge cannot move about, so E inside it can be nonzero.

items.label: Electrostatic equilibrium
items.clue: Condition in which no charge is moving, so E = 0 everywhere inside a metal.

questions.stem: At point P, a charge of +2.0 µC experiences an electric force of 5.0 × 10⁻³ N directed east. This charge is removed and a charge of −6.0 µC is placed at P; the charges that produce the field do not move. Taking east as positive, what is the electric force on the −6.0 µC charge?

Predict first. A solid metal sphere on an insulating stand is touched at one point by a negatively charged rod, which leaves excess electrons on it. Once the sphere has reached electrostatic equilibrium, where is its excess charge?

options.text: Spread evenly through the whole of the sphere's volume
Gathered together at the very center of the sphere
Still at the point where the rod touched the sphere
Spread over the outer surface of the sphere

questions.stem: A hollow metal sphere with inner radius 0.10 m and outer radius 0.20 m carries a charge of +4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. It is isolated, far from other charges, and in electrostatic equilibrium. Point P is in the empty cavity, 0.050 m from the center. Take the potential to be zero far from the sphere, and use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the electric potential at P?

A particle with charge +q is fixed a distance 2d to the left of point P, and a particle with charge +3q is fixed a distance 3d to the right of P. Which expression gives the magnitude of the net electric field at P?

options.text: 2kq/(25d²)
kq/(4d²)
kq/(12d²)

questions.stem: Two spheres of the same size, one metal and one plastic, stand far apart on insulating stands. Each is touched at one point by a negatively charged rod and gains the same small excess charge there. Point P is just outside each sphere, on the side directly opposite the point that was touched. Once each sphere has settled, how does the magnitude of the electric field at P for the metal sphere compare with that for the plastic sphere?

options.text: Equal for the two, since excess charge spreads evenly over any sphere
Greater for the metal sphere, whose excess electrons spread over its surface
Greater for the plastic sphere, as the metal lets its excess charge flow away
Zero for the metal sphere, as the field around a charged conductor is zero

questions.stem: Two metal spheres of different radii are far apart. One is charged and the other is uncharged. They are then connected by a long thin conducting wire. After the charges stop moving, which quantity is the same for the two spheres?

options.text: The electric potential at the surface of each sphere
The amount of excess charge on each of the two spheres
The excess charge per unit area of each sphere's surface
The magnitude of the electric field just outside each sphere

questions.stem: The field lines of a long, straight charged wire spread out radially, in planes at right angles to the wire: they spread in two dimensions, not three. Point P is 2.0 cm from the wire and point Q is 6.0 cm from it, both far from the wire's ends. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 9 times E at Q, as the field strength falls with the square of the distance.
E at P is 3 times E at Q, as the same lines spread over 3 times the area at Q.
E is the same at P and Q, as every line that passes P also passes Q.
E at Q is 3 times E at P, as the larger cylinder at Q holds more lines.

questions.stem: A solid lump of metal with a sharp point at one end carries excess charge and has settled. Which statement is correct?

options.text: E is zero inside the metal near the point; the excess charge is all on the outer surface.
E is strong inside the metal near the point, because the charge crowds toward the point.
E is zero everywhere inside the metal; the excess charge is spread evenly through it.
E is zero only at the centre of the lump; near the point inside, it is not zero.

questions.explanation: In equilibrium no free electron is pushed anywhere inside the metal, so E = 0 at every interior point, whatever the shape. Any excess charge inside would make a field there, so it all sits on the outer surface.

questions.stem: A metal sphere on an insulating stand has a charge of +5.0 nC. It is then connected to Earth by a metal wire, with no other charged objects nearby. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Positive charge flows off the sphere and down the wire into the Earth.
Charge flows until the sphere and the Earth hold equal amounts of charge.
No charge flows, as the neutral Earth exerts no electric force.
Electrons flow from Earth onto the sphere until it is almost neutral.

questions.stem: Sphere A, of radius R, is charged until its potential is V₀ (zero far away). Sphere B, of radius 3R and far from A, is separately charged until it is also at V₀. The two spheres are then joined by a long, thin wire. What happens?

options.text: Charge flows from A to B, because the bigger sphere always takes the larger share.
Charge flows from B to A until the two spheres hold equal charges.
No charge flows, because the spheres are already at the same potential.
Charge flows from A to B until B's potential is 3 times A's.

questions.explanation: Electrons flow only from lower to higher potential (or the reverse for positive charge) until the potentials match. Both are at V₀ already, so nothing moves; B keeps 3 times A's charge.
